transcript.content: Hello. What brings you into the clinic today?

I’m constantly forgetting little everyday things—appointments, errands, even finishing what I start for the community center. My husband and friends were starting to worry it might be early dementia, but my primary care doctor suggested it could actually be a long-standing attention issue, which is why I’m here to see you today.
Have you struggled with these types of attention and forgetfulness since you were a child, or is this a relatively recent change for you?

While these issues have become much more disruptive over the past two years since I retired, I actually struggled with similar things as a child. My elementary school report cards always noted that I daydreamed, rushed, and talked out of turn, and my mother used to scold me for wandering off and leaving chores unfinished.
Since retiring and noticing these changes, have you also been feeling down, depressed, or lost interest in things you normally enjoy?

No, I haven't been feeling depressed or lost interest in my activities at all. If anything, I just feel very frustrated by my forgetfulness and disorganization because I really want to keep up with all the things I enjoy doing.
To help me understand this better, do you have any chronic medical conditions, or did you experience any physical health changes or illnesses around the time your forgetfulness started worsening?

No, I don't have any major chronic medical conditions or physical illnesses. My primary care doctor gave me a thorough checkup and couldn't find any physical cause for these issues, which is why she suggested it might be a long-standing attention problem instead.
Have you ever experienced any head injuries, concussions, or neurological events like a stroke, or noticed any physical symptoms like changes in your balance?
No, I've never had any head injuries, concussions, or strokes in my life. I also haven't noticed any changes in my physical balance; everything seems fine on that front.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with chronic, long-standing symptoms of inattention, forgetfulness, and disorganization that date back to childhood (as evidenced by elementary school report cards noting daydreaming and rushing, and leaving chores unfinished). These symptoms have persisted into adulthood and became more functionally disruptive after retirement. Organic causes (dementia, stroke, head injury) and mood disorders (depression) have been ruled out through clinical history and physical workup by her primary care physician, confirming a diagnosis of Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (F90.0).
